# The website

<a id="website-a-walkthrough-has-one-moment"></a>

## A website walkthrough is written from a brief and shows exactly one moment

`rule:website/a-walkthrough-has-one-moment`

A walkthrough is an interactive, video-like explainer on the website: parts on a stage, a camera, and a
caption for each step, played or stepped through. Each one exists for **one moment**, the step where
what the viewer expected turns out wrong and the feature's point lands.

The scene is written from its **brief**, which its module exports as `brief` (`Brief` in
`website/src/components/walkthrough/engine/brief.ts`) before any step is written:

- `moment`: the one thing the viewer understands at the end, in their words.
- `expectation`: what they expect before it, which the moment corrects.
- `proof`: what on the stage shows the moment is true.
- `leavesOut`: true things the scene leaves out, because they would pull the eye away from the moment.
- `then`: where the viewer goes next.

Exactly one step is written with `moment: true`. The player marks it gold on the scrub bar, its
caption is gold, and the scene slows down for it.

**Everything on the stage serves the moment.** A part, a motion or a caption that is no step toward it
is cut, however true. What is cut is named in `leavesOut`, so the next author knows it was left out on
purpose: the `afterResponse` walkthrough shows no memory or CPU meter, no limit and no failure case. A
second idea is a second walkthrough, and the whole feature is the page `then` names.

A viewer remembers one thing from something they watch. Two moments compete for that one place, and the
stillness and slow motion that make a moment land cannot be spent twice. A brief written first is what
the stage is judged against, and naming what is left out stops the next author from adding it back.

`tools/nv/test/walkthrough-briefs.test.ts` holds every scene under
`website/src/components/walkthrough/scenes/` to the shape: a `brief` with every field filled and exactly
one `moment: true`. Whether the stage serves the moment is a judgement no check makes, and the brief is
where it is written down. The parts gallery, `in-depth/walkthrough-parts`, shows parts and is not a
walkthrough, so it has no brief.

What it spends is coverage: a walkthrough says less than a reference page, and a feature with two
surprises needs two walkthroughs. Nothing of it runs on the request path.

**Declined:**
- **A walkthrough that tours the whole feature.** It becomes a slower reference page, and the reference
  page exists.
- **Memory and CPU meters in the `afterResponse` walkthrough.** They are true, and they pull the eye away
  from the request that is still running.
- **A moment on every step.** When every step is marked, none of them is.

<sub>See also [`testing/website-pages-are-stamped`](testing.md#testing-website-pages-are-stamped).</sub>

<a id="website-a-caption-sits-where-it-happens"></a>

## A walkthrough's caption sits beside what it is about, and the stage slows and blurs the rest while it is read

`rule:website/a-caption-sits-where-it-happens`

A viewer cannot read a caption and watch the stage when the two are apart: the eye goes to one, and
what happens in the other is missed. So a step's caption is a bubble on the stage, beside the part it
is about, with a tail that points at the place where the step happens. `stage.say(part, { side,
point?, focus?, lift?, hold? })` in `website/src/components/walkthrough/engine/stage.ts` places it,
once per step, at the point in the step where it is to be read.

While the caption shows:

- **The panels it is not about blur**, on top of the camera's dimming, so one thing is sharp. `focus`
  names the parts that stay sharp, and by default it is the part the caption points at.
- **The scene slows almost to a stop** (`Timeline.hold`) for a slow reader's time: 0.7 s and 0.24 s a
  word, less the time the words take to arrive. What a scene authors after `say` happens after the
  reading. Whatever already moves keeps moving, slowly, so the frame never freezes.
- **The bubble keeps its size while the camera zooms.** The stage places it in CSS pixels from the
  camera's frame, and its font follows the stage's width. When the part fills the shot, the shot leaves
  `room` on the bubble's side. `lift` moves the bubble away from something next to its point, with a
  line back to the point.

Every frame stays a function of scene time: the hold is a speed track, like the moment's slow motion,
and the speaker-notes window's clock counts it. A step without `say`, such as a step of the parts
gallery, shows its caption at the bottom of the stage.

`tools/nv/test/walkthrough-briefs.test.ts` holds every scene to one `say` per step. Where the bubble
goes in each layout is a judgement no check makes: the frames from `bun nv walkthrough --frames` are
looked at in both layouts and both themes.

What it spends is time and stage: every step lasts longer in real time, and the bubble covers part of
the stage, so a shot leaves room for it. Nothing of it runs on the request path.

**Declined:**
- **Captions under the stage.** The eye leaves the stage to read and misses what moves meanwhile.
- **Stopping the scene for each caption.** A frozen frame looks like a pause or a fault, and the viewer
  would have to press play again.
- **A caption inside the world, scaled by the camera.** Its text size would change with every shot,
  and on a phone's whole-world shot it would be too small to read.

<sub>See also [`website/a-walkthrough-has-one-moment`](website.md#website-a-walkthrough-has-one-moment).</sub>
